https://www.dw.com/en/spain-s-pm-visits-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I40g Spanish authorities were overwhelmed by the latest influx Image: Atlas/REUTERS Advertisement Editors note: For more on the migrant crisis in Ceuta, Spain, follow our blog here . Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez , his interior minister and military personnel were bound for the North African enclave of Ceuta on Friday, a day after thousands of people gained irregular entry to the Spanish territory . At least 18 people died as tens of thousands of people rushed into the small Spanish coastal city, many of them drowning but some also perishing in a stampede to cross the breakwater fence. Authorities are still puzzling over what prompted such large crowds to suddenly seek entry. Regional government head estimates 60,000 new arrivals Preliminary estimates suggest that tens of thousands gained entry on Thursday alone as the Guardia Civil lost control of the border to Morocco . The head of the autonomous city governemnt, Juan Jesus Vivas, estimated that around 60,000 people had arrived, well over half Ceuta's population. "Estimates indicated that around 60,000 people have entered our city as a result of this event," he said. "This figure shows that it is impossible to absorb such pressure. It is absolutely impossible." Around 24 hours earlier, prior to the mass breach, Vivas had issued an esimate of between 1,500 and 2,000. Ceuta's population is roughly 85,000 people. "People are still entering. The reinforcements that have arrived are only helping the injured and other humanitarian efforts," Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers association representing Civil Guard officers, told the Associated Press. Both EFE and AP said correspondents observed some people seeking to return to Morocco on Friday, with the city's small migrant reception center completely overwhelmed. Border police said they had to switch their focus to trying to keep people safe, with at least 18 people killed in the chaos Image: Atlas/REUTERS Spain's PM Sanchez blames traffickers for misrepresenting court ruling Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez arrived in the territory on Friday along with Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska. In a press conference, he called the mass crossings a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity." Sanchez attributed the sudden increase in people seeking to swim around the border to a rumor being spread by human traffickers, deliberately misinterpreting a recent Supreme Court ruling. A Spanish Supreme Court ruled earlier in July that immediate returns of migrants crossing the border illegally did not apply to those arriving by sea. However, the case pertained to people crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Meditereannean Sea, not people swimming around a land border to enter Spain "by sea." "What has emerged from our talks with Moroccan authorities is that trafficking mafias took a self-serving interpretation of a Supreme Court ruling," Sanchez said. Those rumors "spread like wildfire in recent hours," Sanchez added, following the much slower start to the process earlier in the week before Thursday's rush . Spain has two enclaves, Ceuta and Mellila, on the North African coast bordering Morocco. A similar crisis hit Ceuta in 2021 , when more than 8,000 people are thought to have entered irregularly in a matter of days. Italy, Finnish minister question Spain's Schengen status Italy and France both announced they would temporarily boost border checks with Spain. "In response to the situation observed in the Ceuta enclave, I gave instructions as of last night to immediately strengthen the controls at the Spanish border. Furthermore, I am activating the Rapid Intervention Border Force for in-depth checks," French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez wrote online early on Friday. Italian right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had on Thursday called for the "suspension" of Spain's Schengen membership. On Friday, Finland's Interior Minister, a member of the right-wing populist Finns Party that's the second-largest in Helsinki's coalition government, said she supported the proposal. "Spain has completely failed to protect the Schengen Area's external border from infiltration. This cannot continue. All European countries must support Meloni's proposal," Mari Rantanen wrote on Friday. Edited by: Darko Janjevic Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/could-russia-s-gro.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JGBe Cars waiting in line to refuel at a Rosneft gas station in Moscow on August 17 Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS Advertisement Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have triggered a new fuel crisis in Russia . Reuters news agency reports that at least 30 regions are now affected. Unlike the previous wave of shortages, which began in late May and lasted until mid-July, the current crisis is particularly affecting Moscow and the surrounding area, as is apparent from posts on social media. The gas station chains Gazprom Neft and Tatneft have already restricted the sale of fuel in the capital. "You can't say there isn't any fuel. But it's obvious there's a crisis," says Oleg Grigorenko, editor-in-chief of the Russian independent media portal 7x7 , which Russia has branded a "foreign agent." "It's not just a personal problem if you leave the city and don't know whether you can get back again, for example. It's also an economic problem," Grigorenko reports that in several regions taxi drivers, courier services and the construction industry are already losing business, as many of their supply chains are fuel-dependent. "The logistics of private construction companies is heavily reliant on gasoline," Grigorenko explains. People are also having to queue for hours at gas stations in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, according to local media. The authorities are blaming this on a supposed increase in demand during the holiday period. But many locals are saying that this summer season is a disaster. Real estate agent Igor Zakharchenko, from Sochi on the Black Sea coast, wrote on Instagram: "With its quiet atmosphere and leisurely pace of life, Sochi today is reminiscent of the time before the Olympic Games, when there were still not many cars on the roads and the city had far fewer holidaymakers and inhabitants. But the thing is: There's no gas in Sochi." Poor quality fuel Speaking on the Russian broadcaster RTVI, Igor Ananskikh, first deputy chairman of the energy committee in the Russian parliament, said he expected the gas supply situation to normalize within two to three weeks. After waiting hours to fill up, many drivers have found their cars won't start as poor quality fuel has damaged the engine Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS Economist Nikolai Korzhenevsky says this is unlikely. He left Russia in protest at Moscow's war against Ukraine and now lives abroad. In an interview with DW, he highlighted the worsening quality of fuel in Russia. Acquaintances had sent him photos of their cars displaying error messages that indicate engine damage caused by impurities in the fuel. "The car won't start and has to go to the garage. The same people are telling me garages have waitlists of several months, even in Moscow," Korzhenevsky says. "And then you have to wait again for months for replacement parts. Obviously some vehicles can't handle the gasoline that's being put in their tanks." He sees the ongoing problems in the oil and gas industry as harbingers of a much larger and lasting crisis. Russia's oil exports have fallen more sharply during the war than ever before, Bloomberg news has reported. Oil production has also dropped. "In 2019, Russia produced 11.5 million barrels per day," says Korzhenevsky. "Today it's less than 9 million. If this trend continues, and the problems with oil refining get worse, production may fall to 8 million barrels. That would create the conditions for a complete economic and systemic crisis." He doesn't see any quick solution to these problems. In fact he sees Russia going down a similar route to Venezuela , an economy with national income in chronic decline. Hoping for imports is illusory The Russian authorities propose to remedy the fuel shortages with imports from India, China or other countries. But Vyacheslav Shiryaev, a Russian business journalist who also now lives abroad, says this is not viable. Fuel distribution is being restricted due to the lack of supply Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS Given Russia's current isolation, it's impossible to ensure a daily supply of 200,000 tonnes of fuel, which is the approximate amount of gasoline and diesel Russia needs every day, he told DW. Shiryaev, who publicly opposed the war in Ukraine, is also on the Russian authorities' list of so-called "foreign agents." Another Russian economist on that list is Igor Lipsits. He told DW that the damaged refineries cannot quickly be restored and will be vulnerable to further air attacks. This, he says, is why the authorities are already restricting fuel consumption. Municipal services vehicles — medical and rescue workers, police, firefighters — are allowed to jump the line and fill up and so are security personnel and the authorities. "This is happening in front of people who've waited for hours and it's causing a lot of resentment," says Lipsits, a Kremlin critic who left his teaching post at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow because of increasing political pressure. He too now lives in exile in Europe. To Lipsits, the current developments in Russia are strongly reminiscent of the collapse of the Soviet Union . "There were special supply systems for the elite, their own shops and warehouses where they could buy everything they wanted without much difficulty, without waiting in line, and at relatively low prices. That made Russians very angry," he recounts. "When Boris Yeltsin announced that he was going to abolish these closed distribution centers, the people enthusiastically supported him. We are now in a similar situation." Lipsits says a closed system for fuel distribution is evolving in Russia that will make it a luxury to be able to drive a car. The key to ending the war? The economist Shiryaev believes Ukrainian attacks on Russian targets that serve both a military and a civilian purpose could cripple the Russian economy and hasten the end of the war. He believes it would end in just a few weeks if the West supported Ukraine in doubling or tripling the intensity of its attacks. "Ukraine could bring about disorganization and chaos in the Russian interior, resulting in a total loss of control,"Shiryaev says. Russia’s oil empire under pressure To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio He also thinks the fuel shortage could have a decisive role in undermining the stability of Vladimir Putin 's regime. "If there's no diesel, Russia's 6,000-kilometer railway network comes to a halt," he says. "It could also cripple hundreds of factories and businesses. Without diesel, tens of thousands of trucks would be unable to run, food wouldn't get to the stores, and farmers wouldn't be able to harvest their crops." Shiryaev says all this could result in curtailing Putin's plans to continue the war. "If Ukraine destroys the whole oil refining infrastructure, Putin will find that, when he gives an order, it isn't implemented," the economist predicts. Everything will grind to a halt for lack of fuel. This article was originally written in Russian. https://www.dw.com/en/two-people-killed-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NMZs Emergency services rushed to the scene of the crash in Buchloe, Bavaria near the Austrian border Image: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Two people were killed and many more injured when a bus carrying a group of Filipino tourists overturned in southern Germany on Sunday en route to the Munich Oktoberfest . The bus was coming from Milan, an Italian city with a large Filipino community. According to German police, there were 33 tourists on the bus when, at 5:41 a.m. local time (03:41 a.m. GMT), the vehicle went off the side of the A96 highway and overturned. No other vehicles were involved in the crash. Six of the injured were immediately rushed by helicopter to nearby hospitals, one of whom was thought to still be in a life-threatening condition. Two more were taken by ambulance to the hospital, while another 22 were first treated at the scene before several of those were also brought to the hospital. Police so far have only identified one of the two people who died as a 58-year-old Filipino citizen. "It is naturally very chaotic at first, and establishing the facts is difficult,” explained a spokesperson for the local police headquarters. It took police hours to confirm how many people actually were on the bus. Bus driver charged with negligent homicide In addition to the 33 tourists, there were the two Italian bus drivers on board, both of whom were not injured in the crash. The driver who was at the wheel at the time of the crash is now being investigated for negligent homicide, police said. "That is standard procedure,” a police spokeswoman explained. The cause of the accident remained unclear, police said. "The public prosecutor's office has commissioned an accident reconstruction expert report to determine the cause of the crash. It is far too early to comment.” More than 200 firefighters, medics and police were rushed to the scene of the crash. A section of the highway was completely blocked for some time before, but in the afternoon, traffic was allowed to resume. There have been a string of bus accidents in recent weeks. Earlier in September, a Dutch coach crashed in Switzerland , killing five, while a bus crash on Germany's A3 highway left 30 people injured. Oktoberfest draws millions of visitors Munich’s Oktoberfest is the world’s largest beer festival, attracting millions of visitors to the Bavarian capital each year. Held over roughly two weeks, it combines giant beer tents, traditional Bavarian food, live music and fairground rides, drawing visitors from Germany and around the world. This year, the Oktoberfest runs from September 19 to October 4. Organizers said that at the halfway point, around 3.8 million people had already visited the festival — about 300,000 more than at the same point last year. The Oktoberfest is the world's biggest beer festival and draws millions of international tourists Image: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance Edited by: Wesley Dockery If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/16/mili.text: Iran targeted at least 24 commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz in a two-week period, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said on Thursday, as two US aircraft carriers operate in the Arabian Sea and officials on both sides issue public warnings of a possible return to large-scale hostilities.Britain's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a Royal Navy body that monitors merchant shipping safety, reported at least seven further incidents between Monday and Wednesday.The Washington-based think tank said the attacks show Iran still retains the ability to target shipping despite US strikes on its military infrastructure, and cited a US military official as saying Iranian naval forces have adapted by using small boats and spotters to identify vessels after significant damage to their radar systems.In Tehran, senior military officials have issued warnings in recent days. Major General Mostafa Izadi, deputy commander of the IRGC, said on Thursday that Iran "is advancing with strength and is ready to carry out the most powerful operations."Guards spokesman Hossein Mohibi said on Wednesday that a new war against Iran "would be irrational for the United States" but that "the possibility of such a conflict absolutely exists."Iranian army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami said the armed forces were ready for "any battle" and warned that any attack on Iranian infrastructure would bring proportional strikes on Israeli and allied targets.Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, told Press TV on Sunday that US targets including data centres and AI infrastructure would be "within range" if hostilities resumed, and described Washington's latest diplomatic response as insufficient.Washington increases naval presenceThe US Naval Institute confirmed on Tuesday that the aircraft carriers George Washington and George HW Bush are operating in the Arabian Sea.The HW Bush returned to the region after a port visit to Thailand's Phuket. The George Washington had previously relieved the carrier Abraham Lincoln.Their simultaneous presence is significant, though it does not by itself signal an imminent operation given the regular cycle of carrier rotations.US Central Command (CENTCOM) has published images of an F-15E being refuelled mid-air by a KC-135 over the Middle East, flight operations from the George Washington, and an F-35B taking off from the amphibious assault ship Boxer.CENTCOM also said US forces had altered the routes of 130 commercial vessels under the naval blockade of Iran as of 5 October. That figure comes solely from the US military and has not been independently verified.US President Donald Trump said in an interview earlier this month that intensifying air strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November was possible, although he declined to detail any military plans.Asked about reports that his administration was considering renewed use of the GBU-43/B — the Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, known as the "mother of all bombs" — Trump did not dismiss the idea, saying it "is not nuclear; it is simply a very large bomb."He also said future nuclear disarmament talks with Iran involving Russia and China were a possibility.Specialist flight-tracking account IntelSky reported on Wednesday that US Air Force tanker sorties over the region in the first 14 days of October were running at roughly 50% above the daily rate recorded in September.The account reported a similar increase in transport aircraft activity. IntelSky's figures have not been independently verified as publicly available tracking systems do not capture all military aviation, and changes in radar coverage can affect such comparisons.On 1 October, reports claimed that the US military was sending around 9,000 troops and sailors to the region with the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the amphibious ready group centred on the Makin Island.A US official told AP on condition of anonymity that the deployment could bring the total number of American sailors and Marines in the region above 20,000. As of Wednesday, the Theodore Roosevelt had not yet reached the Arabian Sea, according to the Naval Institute.Israel's Channel 12 reported on Thursday citing security sources that Western countries had detected new and unusual military movements inside Iran, but that current events did not necessarily require immediate military action.The channel also reported that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had spoken about the latest developments.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/08/us-f.text: The US military said on Saturday that its forces had "disabled" a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its civilian crew "ignored repeated warnings" and made a number of attempts to "violate" the naval blockade of Iran."A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, disabling the ship after CENTCOM forces directed the crew to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement, adding that it was continuing to "strictly enforce" the blockade against Iran.According to the military command, since July, US forces have redirected 147 commercial vessels that complied with the blockade, while disabling five merchant ships that refused."Additionally, CENTCOM has previously destroyed another 10 Iranian commercial oil tankers that were part of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps’ multibillion-dollar shadow network," it added.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said late on Saturday that it had received a report of an incident involving a bulk carrier and military forces in the Gulf of Oman, around 18 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan on the east coast of the United Arab Emirates.The UAE National Guard announced early on Sunday that 22 people had been rescued from a cargo ship in the gulf.IRGC: Two tankers strike mines around Strait of HormuzAt the same time, Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) navy claimed in a statement that two oil tankers, one to the east of the Strait of Hormuz and the other sailing in the strategic waterway, had caught fire after hitting mines.The Guards said they had been using an "unauthorised" route."These two tankers, through multiple violations and by switching off their navigation and positioning systems, intended to transit the Strait of Hormuz via an unauthorised route. After hitting a mine, they exploded and are burning," the IRGC navy said in a statement.The Guards also accused CENTCOM's commander of "fantasy" and warned that any ship or vessel that cooperates with the US military, "disobeys Iranian regulations for the Strait of Hormuz and enters the unauthorised area, will inevitably hit a mine."Tensions between Tehran and Washington over the Strait of Hormuz have flared once again in recent days following the end of the US midterm elections.On Friday night, reports emerged of explosions on Qeshm Island, and the Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck the area.A few hours later, US President Donald Trump confirmed that US forces had targeted an Iranian air defence system.Iranian news agencies reported on Saturday night that further explosions had been heard in Qeshm, Sirik, Jask and Bandar Abbas.
